FINDING: HTTP query overhead is roughly CONSTANT at ~100-140us per request, not proportional — +44% when the scan is only 305us, but +1.4% once it is milliseconds. So the server is essentially free for real-sized corpora and only visible on tiny ones. INGEST is the real cost: ~14k vec/s over HTTP vs 139-169k in-process, a 10-12x penalty that DOES scale with volume, i.e. JSON float encoding dominates. Recall stays 100.0% both ways, so the HTTP path does not distort results. Anyone quoting nidus throughput must quote the row matching how they run it; this also quantifies what a binary wire format could buy on ingest.

FIXED (v0.33.0). The reported symptom was already resolved by the Clone-on-owning-guard fix in PR #58 — the repro passes 3/3 in isolation and in the full parallel suite, with tracing showing the writer renewing every ~2.7s and the standby correctly reading age=0-3s against its 8s TTL. The 'second defect' was diagnosed from pre-fix evidence (and the confusing ttl=2 line was a concurrently-running test: LOCK_TTL_SECS is 2).

Investigating with pid-tagged lease tracing (NIDUS_LEASE_DEBUG=1, kept in-tree) surfaced four REAL protocol defects that could each produce the same two-owners symptom. All four are fixed, each guarded by a test verified to fail without the fix:

1. RENEWAL WAS A READ-MODIFY-WRITE RACE. renew_lease_object did get-then-UNCONDITIONAL-put, so a peer that reclaimed the lease between the holder's read and its write was silently overwritten — the holder stamped its own ownership back and carried on, while the peer also believed it held the lease. Now a put_cas gated on the token from the same read. A lost CAS is re-read before concluding anything, so an instance racing ITS OWN other renewer (op-driven vs the server timer) is not fenced by mistake.

2. STALENESS MATH WAS OFF BY UP TO A SECOND. Stamps are whole seconds, so an age computed from two truncated stamps can overstate real elapsed time by nearly 1s; a strict age<ttl declared a live, renewing holder dead. Now age<=ttl (see is_live). Takeover lands in ttl..=ttl+1s.

3. A TRANSIENT BACKEND ERROR PERMANENTLY FENCED A HEALTHY WRITER. check_writable latched fenced on ANY renew error, so one dropped connection retired the instance for good. Now only the typed LeaseLost signal latches; a blip fails the write in flight and nothing more.

4. A BACKGROUND RENEWAL LOSS WAS ONLY PRINTED. fenced was latched solely by a failing write, so a superseded writer with no traffic kept answering /ready 200 and reporting holds_writer_handle=true indefinitely — exactly the two-owners window. LeaseRenewer now shares the store's fenced latch (Arc<AtomicBool>).

The repro is folded into the normal suite un-gated (assertions unchanged, plus a new explicit holds_writer_handle assertion), joined by a_superseded_writer_discovers_it_is_fenced_without_any_write. Full cluster suite 14/14, whole e2e target 26/26 against real minio+valkey.

FIXED (v0.34.0). /health now reports 503 when the store lock is poisoned, so liveness restarts the process. No new dependency: the empirical finding recorded in the notes — std poisons only on a WRITE-path panic — ruled out both containment options, since a poisoned store is by construction one whose in-RAM index may not match the durable bytes. clear_poison and CatchPanicLayer would each resume serving from that suspect index; the poison flag is the useful signal and a restart is the remedy.

Readiness checks the same flag (is_poisoned acquires nothing, so it stays off the lock), because otherwise traffic keeps arriving for however long the liveness probe takes to fire. That gap was caught by the test, not by inspection: making readiness lock-free for nidus-abx.3 initially made it blind to poisoning.

Tests: a_poisoned_store_lock_reports_unhealthy_so_liveness_restarts_it, plus a_panic_on_the_read_path_leaves_the_instance_healthy which pins the std semantics the whole design rests on — if read-path panics ever started poisoning, health would begin firing on harmless search panics.

FIXED (v0.34.0). Readiness is answered from atomics only, via a new lock-free Readiness handle (Store::readiness / Nidus::readiness) published into a OnceLock when the store opens. The WouldBlock case is gone from the readiness path entirely rather than tolerated. Store::last_verified became an Arc<AtomicU64> of monotonic millis so staleness is readable without the lock — deliberately monotonic, not SystemTime, since a backwards clock jump would make a reader look younger than it is.

/cluster and /stats keep WouldBlock -> 503: nothing routes on them, so 'momentarily unable to answer' is honest there. The contrast is asserted in the test.

Tests: a_busy_store_is_still_ready (in-process, deterministic — holds the write guard directly) and a_long_write_does_not_make_the_instance_report_unready (real binary, real socket, 10k-record upsert, with a guard assertion so it cannot silently pass by finishing too fast). Both verified to FAIL against the old lock-taking path.

FIXED (v0.34.0), folded into nidus-abx.3 as its design anticipated, since that issue rewrote the same function. The doc comment now describes what readiness actually checks. Swept the modules the lp4 epic touched for the same drift; no other comment names a closed issue as owning future work.

Fixed in PR #62 via --body-idle-timeout: an http_body::Body wrapper that abandons a request body which stops delivering frames (default 15s, 0 disables). IDLE not total, so a large slow upload is never cut off. Permit still held during body arrival (deliberate — bounds concurrent buffering), so the pin window is shortened, not eliminated; proxy-level slow-client defence remains the real answer, as documented. e2e test drives it over a raw socket and was verified to FAIL without the fix. http-body added to Cargo.toml but adds zero packages/build time (axum already depends on the same version); absent from the pure library tree.
